sections.h2: Who handles a Kentucky property tax bill
sections.html:
Four local offices each take one stage. Each stage has its own desk. The property valuation administrator (PVA) puts the value on every parcel. Fall bills come from the sheriff, who also takes the payments. Whatever is still open after April lands with the county clerk, then the county attorney follows up on it.

The PVA aims for fair cash value, which is what a willing buyer and seller would agree on. Each parcel gets a physical review at least every four years, and new construction is added annually. Farmland may be valued as agricultural land. Coal, oil, gas and utility property go to the state Office of Property Valuation instead.

So call the PVA about value, the sheriff about what you owe now, and the clerk about anything that has slipped past April 15. That avoids a lot of phone tag once a sale is underway.

Your first move is a conference with the PVA or a deputy, which can happen by phone on request. If you still disagree afterward, hand the clerk a brief written petition that names the parcel, your reasons and the value you believe is fair.

The roll goes on public display the first Monday in May for 13 days. File no later than the end of the next workday after the display closes. A PVA can request more time, and with state approval the deadline can move out by up to 25 days. Skip the local board, or miss your own hearing, and you lose the later state appeal.

  • The local board of assessment appeals meets 25 to 35 days after the roll closes, with a public hearing on every protest.
  • Proof wins these cases: recent sale or listing prices, building costs, insurance policies, mortgages or loans. A protest backed by nothing must be denied.
  • You may make an audio recording of your hearing.
  • If you hire someone to speak for you, they must hold a role the statute names, such as lawyer, CPA, tax consultant, real estate broker or appraiser, or be your employee, and you must authorize them in writing.

An appeal never freezes the bill. KRS 133.120(9) has you pay based on the value you put in your petition. Should the final value come out higher, the gap plus interest is yours to pay. When bills print before an appeal ends, your claimed value is used and a second bill covers anything the board adds.

Write down what you saw when you walked the property: peeling roof, a cracked foundation, a dated kitchen. Photos and repair quotes carry real weight at a hearing, and the same file helps you explain your asking price to a buyer.

sections.h2: If you lose at the county board
sections.html:
Further review goes to the state tax appeals board under KRS 49.220. It must receive your petition within 30 days after the county board mailed its decision. That board decides the matter anew instead of reading the earlier record.

Any time the county board changes a value it must explain why in writing, and if you or the PVA request it, the board has to visit the parcel. KRS 133.120 was amended in 2026, so read the current wording before you file.

This is the standard schedule. A county that mails bills after November 1 runs a later version, with a 30 day window for each stage.

Standard Kentucky real property schedule
DateWhat happens
Jan. 1Valuation snapshot date
Jan. 1 to Mar. 1Owners may list real property
Early May (first Monday)Roll on display for 13 days
Oct. 1 to Nov. 1Early payers save 2%
Nov. 2 to Dec. 31Face amount due
All of January5% added
Feb. 1 to Apr. 1521% added
End of day Apr. 15Unpaid bills leave the sheriff for the clerk

Listing is not an annual chore when last year's roll described your land and buildings completely and accurately and nothing big has changed.

For a homeowner planning a spring listing, the practical dates are early October and the turn of the year. Paying in October trims the bill and leaves a clean record for the buyer's title search, while waiting until January means a surcharge that a closing agent will expect to see paid off at the table.

Every taxing body chooses its own rate, within House Bill 44. It may drop to the compensating rate, which holds revenue from existing property level. It may also pick a rate that grows that revenue by at most 4 percent, after a public hearing. Anything higher invites a voter petition and a possible recall vote. Rates are written as cents per $100 of value.

The state's own 2025 real property rate, announced by the Department of Revenue, is 10.6 cents per $100 of assessed value, lower than the 10.9 of the year before. State revenue growth from existing property is capped at 4 percent. Cities, school districts, counties and special districts each layer on a rate of their own, so what you pay depends on the parcel's address.

sections.h2: What happens when a bill goes unpaid
sections.html:
Once April 15 passes, your unpaid bill turns into a certificate of delinquency, which is a lien on the parcel. Costs then stack up stage by stage.

  • Interest accrues at 1 percent a month.
  • The clerk adds a 10 percent fee and the attorney adds 20 percent, though the attorney's portion is waived for an owner who pays within five business days after the clerk receives the list.
  • Notices come from the county attorney, one by May 15 and another by June 15, with payment plan offers included.
  • Certificate sales to private buyers start in mid-July and can continue into late October, though most wrap up by the end of August.

The thing sold is the lien, not the house. You remain the owner, but the investor now holds the debt and adds fees of its own.

sections.h2: Selling with taxes owed or due
sections.html:
Know your balance before you put a sign in the yard. Ask the sheriff what the current bill is, and ask the clerk whether any certificate of delinquency is attached to the parcel. A county has to publish its delinquent list online and in the newspaper at least 30 days ahead of a sale.

As the seller you also owe the real estate transfer tax of $0.50 per $500 of declared value, collected by the clerk when the deed is recorded. Foreclosure transfers and surrenders in lieu of foreclosure are outside it. A homestead exemption on the property should be reported to the PVA at transfer. Organizations with a Section 170 exemption, such as churches or libraries, use Revenue Form 62A023.

The title company will search for any open delinquency and pay it out of your proceeds. A cash buyer purchasing as-is follows the same path, with the unpaid balance coming off what you receive, so an early number keeps closing on time.

Pull together the latest bill, a payoff figure from the sheriff or clerk, and the assessed value on file. Set that value beside recent nearby sales. If it looks too high while the display window is open, a free conference with the PVA could lower it for the next owner as well.

faqs.q: When does a Kentucky property tax bill arrive and when is it due?
faqs.a: Bills go out from the sheriff in the fall, and collection opens October 1 or November 1 depending on the county. Pay through November 1 for a 2 percent discount. Face value is accepted through December 31.

faqs.q: Until what day can I protest my valuation?
faqs.a: File one workday after the 13 day display period closes. Display begins the first Monday in May, and you need to meet with the PVA first.

faqs.q: What penalties hit a late Kentucky bill?
faqs.a: All of January adds 5 percent. From February 1 to April 15 the add-on is 21 percent. After that the clerk takes over and 1 percent monthly interest and more fees apply.

faqs.q: Can the county sell my home over unpaid tax?
faqs.a: The sale covers the lien, a certificate of delinquency, not the house. You keep title but owe whoever bought the certificate.

faqs.q: Who fixes the state real property rate?
faqs.a: The Department of Revenue, each year by July 1 under KRS 132.020. The 2025 figure is 10.6 cents per $100 of assessed value.
